hints.title: Squaring Monotonic Extremum Obstacle
hints.text: Squaring each number disrupts sorted order because negative numbers yield large positive squares. Sorting after squaring takes logarithmic factor overhead. Given that the largest squares must originate at either the far left or far right, how can you build the result in linear time?

hints.title: Extremum Inward Convergence
hints.text: Compare the squared values at the outer ends of the array. The larger square belongs at the end of the output buffer; fill the result from right to left.

hints.title: Backward Fill Procedure
hints.text: Allocate an output array of length n. Set left to zero, right to n minus one, and write pointer pos to n minus one. Compute squares of values at left and right. Put the larger square at res[pos], advance the chosen boundary pointer, and decrement pos until all positions are filled.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```python
class Solution:
    def sortedSquares(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        n = len(nums)
        res = [0] * n
        left, right = 0, n - 1
        pos = n - 1
        while left <= right:
            left_sq = nums[left] * nums[left]
            right_sq = nums[right] * nums[right]
            if left_sq > right_sq:
                res[pos] = left_sq
                left += 1
            else:
                res[pos] = right_sq
                right -= 1
            pos -= 1
        return res
```

variables: N: length of nums array (1 <= N <= 10^4)
complexity.notes: Two-pointer backward fill in O(N) time with O(N) output memory.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Squaring elements and calling an O(N log N) sorting routine misses the pre-existing sorted property of the input array.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Filling from highest to lowest square achieves optimal O(N) time without extra passes.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Explaining why the maximum square is always at one of the two ends (parabolic property of x^2 centered at 0).
